contents.name: Bühler–Salamon Example 3.8(i), p.122; Brezis §3.2 definition p.57
contents.locator: Bühler–Salamon Example 3.8(i), p.122; Brezis §3.2 definition p.57
contents.support: For K=R or C and normed X, sigma(X,X*) is the initial topology of all K-linear continuous f:X->K with the usual scalar topology. It agrees with the finite-neighborhood topology used in the published Mazur theorem. No completeness is assumed.

contents.name: Bühler–Salamon Lemma 3.6(i),(ii), pp.119–121; Example 3.8(ii), p.122
contents.support: At x the sets U(x;f_1,...,f_m;epsilon)={y: |f_j(y-x)|<epsilon for every j}, m finite including zero and epsilon>0, form a base. They are convex and balanced at zero. Addition and scalar multiplication are continuous; sigma(X,X*) is coarser than norm topology.

contents.name: Bühler–Salamon Lemma 3.6(iv), p.121; Example 3.8(i), p.122
contents.support: For real or complex normed X, sigma(X,X*) is Hausdorff.

contents.name: Bühler–Salamon Lemma 3.6(iii), p.121; net extension by finite directed upper bounds
contents.locator: Bühler–Salamon Lemma 3.6(iii), p.121; net extension by finite directed upper bounds
contents.support: Write x_i -> x weakly iff f(x_i)->f(x) for every f in X*. This is equivalent to convergence in sigma(X,X*): directedness gives a common upper bound for the finitely many coordinate thresholds. Sequences use the usual directed order on N; closure is topological closure.

contents.name: Bühler–Salamon Example 3.9(i),(ii), p.122
contents.support: Recall sigma(X*,X), already defined on the preceding A page, without rehoming or reminting def-weak-star-topology. On X*, sigma(X*,X) is coarser than sigma(X*,X**) and than norm topology, because evaluations belong to X**. The predual X is part of the notation.

contents.name: Bühler–Salamon Lemma 3.6 and Example 3.9(i), pp.119–122
contents.support: At f0 the sets {|(f-f0)(x_j)|<epsilon, 1<=j<=m} form a neighborhood base, m finite including zero. Sigma(X*,X) is Hausdorff, locally convex, with continuous addition and scalar multiplication.

contents.name: Bühler–Salamon Example 3.9(iii), p.122; finite-coordinate net adaptation
contents.locator: Bühler–Salamon Example 3.9(iii), p.122; finite-coordinate net adaptation
contents.support: A net f_i in X* converges weak-star to f iff f_i(x)->f(x) for every x in X. Finite directed upper bounds prove equivalence with topological convergence. Sequences are a special case, and never define closure.

contents.name: Bühler–Salamon Lemmas 3.13–3.14 and Theorem 3.12(i), pp.125–127; Brezis Lemma 3.2, p.64
contents.locator: Bühler–Salamon Lemmas 3.13–3.14 and Theorem 3.12(i), pp.125–127; Brezis Lemma 3.2, p.64
contents.support: Let V be a K-vector space, f_1,...,f_m and L linear V->K, m finite including zero. If intersection ker f_j is contained in ker L then L=sum a_j f_j for some scalars a_j. Consequently the continuous linear dual of the initial topology generated by any family F of linear functionals is span F.

contents.name: Bühler–Salamon Lemma 3.16, p.127
contents.support: The K-linear continuous functionals on (X,sigma(X,X*)) are exactly X*.

contents.name: Bühler–Salamon Corollary 3.25, p.130; Brezis Proposition 3.14, pp.64–65
contents.locator: Bühler–Salamon Corollary 3.25, p.130; Brezis Proposition 3.14, pp.64–65
contents.support: Every K-linear sigma(X*,X)-continuous L:X*->K has the form L(f)=f(x) for a unique x in X. Conversely every evaluation is weak-star continuous.

contents.name: Bühler–Salamon Lemma 3.15, p.127; Brezis Theorem 3.7, pp.60–61
contents.locator: Bühler–Salamon Lemma 3.15, p.127; Brezis Theorem 3.7, pp.60–61
contents.support: For any convex C in a real or complex normed X, norm closure equals weak closure; in particular norm closed iff weakly closed, including C empty.

contents.name: Bühler–Salamon Lemma 3.21, p.129
contents.support: In infinite-dimensional normed X, the weak closure of {x:||x||=1} is {x:||x||<=1}.

contents.name: Bühler–Salamon Definition 3.17 and Corollary 3.26, pp.128,130
contents.support: For arbitrary M subset X and N subset X*, M-perp is sigma(X*,X)-closed and preannihilator N is sigma(X,X*)-closed; both are linear subspaces.

contents.name: Bühler–Salamon Corollaries 3.18 and 3.26, pp.128,130
contents.support: Reuse the published theorem: preannihilator(M-perp)=norm closure M=weak closure M for linear M<=X, while (preannihilator N)-perp=weak-star closure N for linear N<=X*. Do not replace the last closure by norm closure.

contents.name: Bühler–Salamon Exercise 3.60(a) p.161 (ell-two case); Example 1.34 pp.34–35 (ell-p extension)
contents.locator: Bühler–Salamon Exercise 3.60(a) p.161 (ell-two case); Example 1.34 pp.34–35 (ell-p extension)
contents.support: For real ell^p, 1<p<infinity, e_n converges weakly to 0 although ||e_n||_p=1.

contents.name: Bühler–Salamon Exercise 3.61(a), p.161
contents.support: The coordinate vectors of real ell^1 do not converge weakly to 0.

contents.name: Bühler–Salamon Example 3.9(iii), p.122 and Example 1.35, p.36
contents.locator: Bühler–Salamon Example 3.9(iii), p.122 and Example 1.35, p.36
contents.support: In real (ell^1)*=ell-infinity, f_n(x)=x_n converges weak-star to zero, with ||f_n||=1.

contents.name: Bühler–Salamon Exercise 3.61(a),(b), p.161
contents.support: In real ell^1=(c0)*, e_n tends weak-star to zero but not weakly to zero.

contents.name: Bühler–Salamon Exercise 3.60(b), p.161
contents.support: In real ell^2, A={sqrt(n+1)e_n:n>=0} is sequentially weakly closed, but 0 belongs to its weak closure and not to A.

contents.name: Bühler–Salamon Example 2.6 p.61, combined with Example 3.9(iii) p.122
contents.locator: Bühler–Salamon Example 2.6 p.61, combined with Example 3.9(iii) p.122
contents.support: Let E=c00 with supremum norm and f_n(x)=(n+1)x_n. Then f_n converges weak-star to zero in E*, but ||f_n||=n+1. In particular pointwise boundedness on incomplete E does not bound operator norms.

contents.name: Example 3.3: smooth-function locally convex topology
contents.reason: General Frechet smooth-function spaces require the later locally convex development; no proof on this pair uses that example. No general locally convex A/B destination exists in the current plan; these independent general-TVS results are not required by FA8 and are not suppliers.

contents.name: Example 3.5: convergence in measure and trivial dual
contents.reason: The nonlocally-convex measurable-function topology is not needed for either normed dual pairing; it belongs with nonnormable spaces. No general locally convex A/B destination exists in the current plan; these independent general-TVS results are not required by FA8 and are not suppliers.

contents.name: Theorem 3.11: separation in general topological vector spaces
contents.reason: The normed separation theorem is already proved. General topological-vector-space separation belongs to the later seminorm development. No general locally convex A/B destination exists in the current plan; these independent general-TVS results are not required by FA8 and are not suppliers.

contents.name: Exercise 3.22 and Exercise 3.61(c): Schur theorem
contents.reason: This independent sequence theorem is not assumed for the selected ell-two closure counterexample. It belongs to the later Banach-space sequence package.

contents.name: Exercise 3.23: bounded sets with separable dual
contents.reason: Metrizability and sequential closure on bounded sets are part of the compactness and separability development.

contents.name: Corollary 3.29: Goldstine
contents.reason: Goldstine has its own next A/B pair and is not imported to establish the present weak or weak-star topology.

contents.name: Lemma 3.10: convex closure and interior
contents.reason: The general TVS interior assertion is an independent generalization; only normed convex closure is consumed here through the published Mazur theorem.

contents.name: Example 3.4: indiscrete/discrete vector topology
contents.reason: This general TVS example is not one of the required weak-topology distinctions and supplies no prerequisite.

contents.name: Example 3.7: products as initial linear topologies
Lemma 3.20: Mazur convex-combination approximation
contents.reason: The closed-convex topology dictionary uses separation directly; a new sequential approximation theorem is not required by this design and is not used.

contents.name: Corollary 3.27: weak-star convex separation
contents.reason: The next compactness pair needs separation for Goldstine; the current linear-subspace closure formula already has its finite-coordinate proof.

contents.name: Corollary 3.28: dual unit sphere weak-star closure
Example 1.35: ell-one does not exhaust ell-infinity dual
contents.reason: The systematic extra functionals on ell-infinity require the later Banach-limit and finitely additive dual discussion.

contents.name: Brezis §3.2 Example 1 and footnote 2, p.59
contents.support: Every weak neighborhood of x in an infinite-dimensional normed X contains x+K v for some nonzero v, and is therefore norm unbounded.

contents.name: Brezis Proposition 3.5(iii), p.58 (completeness needed only for the dual)
contents.locator: Brezis Proposition 3.5(iii), p.58 (completeness needed only for the dual)
contents.support: Assume AC_omega in addition to the inherited Hahn–Banach machinery. If x_n converges weakly in a normed X, sup_n ||x_n||<infinity. X itself need not be complete.

contents.name: Brezis Proposition 3.5(iii), p.58; net form by the same dual norm estimate
contents.locator: Brezis Proposition 3.5(iii), p.58; net form by the same dual norm estimate
contents.support: For every weakly convergent net x_i->x, ||x||<=liminf_i ||x_i||, with liminf=sup_i inf_{j>=i} in the extended nonnegative reals. Every norm sublevel set is weakly closed.

contents.name: Brezis Proposition 3.6 and Examples 1–2, pp.58–60
contents.support: The weak and norm topologies of a real or complex normed X agree iff X is finite-dimensional.

contents.name: Brezis Exercise 3.8(1)–(3), p.81; local-base version and published ZF no-countable-basis route
contents.locator: Brezis Exercise 3.8(1)–(3), p.81; local-base version and published ZF no-countable-basis route
contents.support: Assume AC_omega and the inherited dual-separation principle. The weak topology of an infinite-dimensional normed X is not first countable at zero (hence at any point).

contents.name: Brezis §3.3 Theorem 3.10, p.61, forward direction
contents.support: For bounded T:X->Y between normed spaces, T:(X,weak)->(Y,weak) is continuous, and T*:(Y*,sigma(Y*,Y**))->(X*,sigma(X*,X**)) is continuous.

contents.name: Brezis Exercise 3.10 p.81 and Proposition 3.14 pp.64–65, combined preadjoint consequence
contents.locator: Brezis Exercise 3.10 p.81 and Proposition 3.14 pp.64–65, combined preadjoint consequence
contents.support: For normed X,Y, bounded T:X->Y has weak-star continuous transpose T*:Y*->X*. Conversely a bounded weak-star continuous K-linear S:Y*->X* equals T* for a unique bounded T:X->Y, with ||T||<=||S|| (hence equality by transpose norm equality).

contents.name: Brezis §3.2 Example 1 footnote 2, p.59; explicit net adaptation of unbounded weak neighborhoods
contents.locator: Brezis §3.2 Example 1 footnote 2, p.59; explicit net adaptation of unbounded weak neighborhoods
contents.support: Every infinite-dimensional normed space has a weakly null net whose norms tend to infinity; no tail is norm bounded.

contents.name: Corollary 3.8: Mazur combinations
contents.reason: This is an independent sequential approximation consequence and is not needed for the commissioned topology comparison proofs.

contents.name: Corollary 3.9 and Remark 6: convex lower semicontinuity
Theorem 3.10 converse and Remark 7 continuity equivalences
contents.reason: The converse for arbitrary linear maps between Banach spaces is a closed-graph application; this design specifies bounded transposes and their weak-star preadjoints, and does not consume that converse.

contents.name: Exercise 3.8(4): nonmetrizable weak-star topology on infinite-dimensional Banach predual
contents.reason: The assigned countability theorem concerns weak topology on normed X; the weak-star analogue has a different Banach-predual hypothesis and is not needed.

contents.name: Feldman, Operator Topologies, Definition 1 p.1; Banach-space/net adaptation
contents.locator: Feldman, Operator Topologies, Definition 1 p.1; Banach-space/net adaptation
contents.support: On B(X,Y), SOT is the initial topology of T->Tx into normed Y for all x in X; WOT is the initial topology of T->g(Tx) into K for x in X,g in Y*. Thus nets converge in SOT iff pointwise in norm and in WOT iff pointwise weakly. Finite tests form neighborhood bases; neither is named simply the weak topology of B(X,Y).

contents.name: Feldman, Operator Topologies, Remark 2 p.1
contents.support: For nets of bounded operators between normed spaces, operator norm convergence implies SOT convergence, which implies WOT convergence.

contents.name: Feldman, Operator Topologies, Example 3(c), p.2
contents.support: On real ell^2, R(x_0,x_1,...)=(0,x_0,x_1,...) has R^n->0 in WOT but not SOT.

contents.name: Feldman, Operator Topologies, Example 3(a),(b), pp.1–2
contents.support: On real ell^2, L(x_0,x_1,...)=(x_1,x_2,...) has L^n->0 in SOT and ||L^n||=1.

contents.name: Example 4: multiplication failures
contents.reason: Joint multiplication continuity and its mixed variants are independent operator-algebra extensions; the design asks for the two shift convergence distinctions.

contents.name: Example 5: Hilbert adjoints
contents.reason: Hilbert adjoints need the later Hilbert Riesz theorem; the present transpose is the bilinear Banach transpose.

contents.name: Theorem 6(a)–(d): operator bounds and product convergence
contents.reason: These operator-family results go beyond the commissioned comparison and examples; none is used to establish the shift calculations or weak-net distinction.
